contests.title: Jackson County Question 1 — Anti-crime sales-tax continuation

provenance.sourceOrg: Jackson County Board of Election Commissioners
provenance.quote:
JACKSON COUNTY, MISSOURI
              QUESTION # 1
Shall Jackson County continue its anti-crime sales tax,
commonly known as COMBAT, at the rate of one-quarter
of one cent for a period of ten years for the purpose of
promoting and providing public safety within Jackson
County, including the prevention and treatment of drug
abuse and addiction and the prevention, investigation,
prosecution, and detention of violent criminals and drug
dealers? The proceeds of this tax shall be deposited in a
special Jackson County Anti-Crime Sales Tax Trust
Fund, separate from the general fund or any other county
funds.
YES
NO
       JACKSON COUNTY MISSOURI

provenance.sourceOrg: Jackson County Board of Election Commissioners
provenance.quote:
CITY OF BLUE SPRINGS, MO
               QUESTION
Shall the City of Blue Springs, Missouri impose a local
use tax at the same rate as the total local sales tax rate,
currently 2.5%, provided that if the local sales tax rate is
reduced or raised by voter approval, the local use tax rate
shall also be reduced or raised by the same action?
If this question is approved, the City of Blue Springs
would begin collecting a use tax from sales made to Blue
Springs buyers by online and out of state vendors that
are not currently taxed. The funds derived from the use
tax will fund streets and other capital improvements.
YES
NO

measures.officialStatement:
A “yes” vote will repeal Article I, Section 36, of the Missouri Constitution approved by the voters in 2024 which provided reproductive healthcare rights, including abortion through fetal viability; continue to ensure women’s ability to access medical care for medical emergencies, ectopic pregnancies, and miscarriages; allow legislation to regulate abortion providers and facilities to ensure health and safety; require informed and voluntary consent for an abortion, including parental or judicial consent for minors; allow restriction of abortions to cases of medical emergency, rape and incest under twelve weeks gestation, and fetal anomalies; prohibit public funding of abortions except in limited circumstances; and prohibit gender transition procedures for minors including gender transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones or puberty-blocking drugs, with exceptions for specific medical conditions.
A “no” vote will leave Article I, Section 36, of the Missouri Constitution approved by voters in 2024 in place; will not limit abortion to cases of medical emergency, rape and incest under twelve weeks gestation, and fetal anomalies, but leave access to abortion available through fetal viability; will not prohibit gender transition procedures for minors.
If passed, this measure will not increase or decrease taxes.

A “yes” vote will prohibit the people’s elected representatives from directly amending or changing any law enacted through the initiative process; require that any modifications to laws enacted through the initiative process be referred to the people by a vote of at least 80% of each chamber of the General Assembly; restrict the legislature from passing laws that limit the ability to pursue initiatives and referenda; maintain the current signature requirements of five percent of the individual legal voters in each of two-thirds of Missouri’s congressional districts for proposing a law; maintain the current signature requirement of eight percent of individual legal voters in each of two-thirds of Missouri’s congressional districts for proposing a constitutional amendment; and maintain the current requirement that a simple statewide majority of votes cast on a measure by individual legal voters is sufficient to enact any law or constitutional amendment.
A “no” vote will not change the current constitutional provisions, which already give citizens the right to propose initiatives and referenda.
If passed, this measure will not increase or decrease taxes.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Continues Jackson County’s COMBAT anti-crime sales tax at one-quarter of one cent for ten years. The money would support public safety, including prevention and treatment of drug abuse and addiction and prevention, investigation, prosecution and detention of violent criminals and drug dealers. Revenue would go into a separate Jackson County Anti-Crime Sales Tax Trust Fund.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the ten-year continuation of the COMBAT tax for these purposes.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed ten-year continuation of the COMBAT tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Imposes a Blue Springs local use tax at the same rate as the city’s total local sales tax, currently 2.5%. If voters later raise or lower that sales-tax rate, the use-tax rate would change with it. The city would collect the use tax on purchases by Blue Springs buyers from online and out-of-state sellers that are not currently taxed. Revenue would fund streets and other capital improvements.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the local use tax, with its rate tied to the local sales-tax rate and revenue used for streets and other capital improvements.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed local use tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorizes Independence to issue $19.9 million in general obligation bonds to renovate, improve and equip historic buildings, facilities and grounds and create a 20-year business plan for historic buildings. Priority would go to the Bingham-Waggoner Estate, Vaile Mansion, Truman Memorial Building, Old Fire Station One and 1827 Log Courthouse. The 20-year period describes the business plan.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the $19.9 million bond issue for these historic-property projects and business plan.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Asks whether Lee’s Summit should provide residential solid waste collection services throughout the city.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the city providing residential solid waste collection services city-wide.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the proposal for the city to provide residential solid waste collection services city-wide.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Repeals Missouri’s 2024 constitutional reproductive-freedom section and replaces it with a new section. Abortion would be allowed for a medical emergency, a fetal anomaly that makes life outside the womb impossible, rape or incest; rape and incest abortions would be limited to no later than twelve weeks of gestation. The legislature could regulate abortion care, facilities and providers. Except when a medical emergency prevents consent, abortion would require voluntary, informed consent. For an unemancipated minor under 18, the physician would need written consent from the minor and a parent or legal guardian and would keep it in the medical record; the legislature could allow consent by court order. The amendment protects care for miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy and other medical emergencies. It prohibits abortion based on a prenatal disability finding except for a fetal anomaly, and bars public funding for abortion except for medical emergency, rape or incest as otherwise allowed by law. It bans fetal-organ harvesting as defined in the amendment, with exceptions for specified diagnostic, paternity and law-enforcement uses. It prohibits gender-transition surgery, cross-sex hormones and puberty-blocking drugs for people under 18, with exceptions for medically verifiable disorders of sex development and treatment unrelated to gender transition. Challenges to state reproductive-health laws would go to Cole County Circuit Court, with notice to the attorney general when required. If one provision is held invalid, the others would remain in effect.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Adopt the replacement constitutional section with these abortion rules, consent requirements and restrictions on gender-transition procedures for minors.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the replacement section and retain the existing constitutional reproductive-freedom section.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Makes initiative and referendum powers fundamental constitutional rights and allows courts to revise ballot summaries through lawsuits. Bars laws that weaken those powers. Lawmakers could not directly amend laws enacted by initiative; proposed changes would have to go back to voters after approval by at least 80% of each chamber. The ballot question also restricts legislation similar to laws rejected by referendum. Existing petition signature requirements and approval by a simple statewide majority would remain.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve these rules, including the requirement that legislative changes to initiative laws go back to voters after approval by at least 80% of each chamber.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the proposed changes; the current constitutional initiative and referendum provisions would remain in place.
